thread.title: Tech sector forfeits half a trillion dollars in value over 2-week span - MarketWatch

author: Anora M. Gaudiano
title: Tech sector forfeits half a trillion dollars in value over 2-week span - MarketWatch
text:
The unwinding of the most crowded trade of the year—big tech—has contributed significantly to a shaving off of half a trillion dollars in total market cap from the S&P 500 technology sector over the past two weeks, according to WSJ Market Data Group.
Considering how high these stocks had climbed over the past year and the business and regulatory challenges that lie ahead for the likes of Facebook, Twitter and Google, investors can expect further weakness in the sector, according to Nicholas Colas, co-founder of DataTrek Research.
The S&P 500 tech sector XLK, -0.68% peaked on March 12 at 1,233.93, putting its market cap at about $6 trillion. By Tuesday’s close, the market cap was down to $5.5 trillion, a decline of 8.8%, according to WSJ Market Data Group.
Much of those losses came from a handful of megastocks such as Alphabet Inc. GOOG, -0.06% GOOGL, -0.19% , Facebook Inc. FB, +0.68% , Apple Inc. AAPL, -1.06% , Microsoft Corp. MSFT, -0.09% and Netflix Inc. NFLX, -4.59% —known collectively as the FAANG stocks. They’ve shed an aggregate $338 billion in value since March 12.
Amazon.com AMZN, -4.99% , which resides in the S&P consumer-discretionary industry but doubles as a big tech stock, has lost $74 billion in market valuation since peaking on March 12.
The weakness in tech stocks is similar to the weakness of the largest stocks in general.
The largest 25 stocks on the S&P 500 SPX, -0.38% , representing just 5% of the index, lost $920 billion in market cap since a broader market peak on Jan. 26, according to Bespoke Investment Group.
“Since Jan. 26, the S&P 500 [has] lost $2.34 trillion in market cap, while the 25 largest stocks have lost nearly a trillion. This means the 25 largest stocks have accounted for roughly 40% of the losses,” Bespoke analysts observed in research note.
While the S&P 500 index is down less than 10% from its peak in January, the average stock on the index is now 15% below its 52-week high, and the average stock in certain sectors is already in or near bear-market territory, defined as a drop of 20%, according to this chart from the Bespoke.
Market Pulse: Amazon.com shares tumble into correction territory on report that the e-commerce giant is in Trump’s crosshairs
Despite the brutal selloff of the past few weeks, technology stocks still are faring better than others on a trailing-12-months basis—a reflection of just how far they had climbed over the past year.
The S&P tech sector is still up 24% over the past 12 months, compared with an 11% gain for the S&P 500.
“With the end of first quarter almost here, Tuesday’s selloff [in tech] is a sign many portfolio managers no longer want to show dramatic overexposure to the group. We doubt they finished selling down these positions,” said Colas in a note.
